sections.title: What are Queues?
sections.content:
A **queue** is a First-In-First-Out (FIFO) data structure. The first element you enqueue is the first element you dequeue. The physical analogy is a line at a ticket counter: the person who arrived first gets served first. Queues appear everywhere real-world ordering matters: print jobs, CPU task scheduling, and network packet processing all use queues.

In JavaScript, queues are typically simulated with arrays using `push` (enqueue to back) and `shift` (dequeue from front). However, `shift` is O(n) because it moves every remaining element one position left in memory. For interview problems with small inputs, this is fine. For large inputs (n ≥ 10⁵), this hidden O(n) cost per dequeue turns a BFS from O(V + E) into O(V² + E). The correct solution is a pointer-based dequeue: maintain a `head` pointer and advance it instead of shifting.

The most important use of queues in algorithms is **Breadth-First Search (BFS)**. BFS explores a graph layer by layer - first all nodes at distance 1 from the source, then distance 2, then distance 3. This layer-by-layer property is guaranteed by the FIFO behavior of the queue: nodes are processed in the order they were discovered, which is exactly the order of increasing distance.

The second important structure is the **deque** (double-ended queue) - a queue that supports O(1) push and pop from both ends. The deque is the backbone of the sliding window maximum and minimum pattern, where we need to efficiently track the extremum of a sliding window.

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: A queue is the right structure any time you need to process items in the order they were discovered or added, and you need the oldest item first. BFS is the clearest trigger - any 'shortest path' on an unweighted graph or grid, any 'level-order traversal' of a tree, and any 'process nodes in layers' problem needs a queue. Sliding window maximum (where monotonic deque applies) and multi-source propagation problems are the other major triggers.
signals: level order traversal of a tree
shortest path in an unweighted graph or grid
multi-source BFS (start from multiple nodes simultaneously)

Core Template
sections.explanation: BFS uses a head pointer instead of shift for O(1) dequeue - the queue array grows but each element is accessed exactly once. Level size is computed at the start of each level (not dynamically) so newly enqueued nodes don't corrupt the current level's count. Monotonic deque maintains decreasing values so the front is always the maximum; expired indices are removed from front, dominated indices from back.

items.name: Priority Queue (Min-Heap)
items.description: A priority queue dequeues the minimum (or maximum) priority element rather than the oldest. JavaScript has no built-in priority queue - implement with a min-heap. Used for Dijkstra's shortest path and the Kth largest element. Covered in the Heaps topic.
items.example_problem: Kth Largest Element in a Stream

items.name: Circular Queue
items.description: A queue implemented with a fixed-size array that wraps around using modulo arithmetic. When the tail pointer reaches the array end, it wraps to index 0. Avoids the need for a dynamic array. `Design Circular Queue` on LeetCode is the direct practice problem.

items.name: Multi-Source BFS
items.description: Enqueue all source nodes before starting the BFS loop. Each source is at distance 0; all other nodes are reached by whichever source is nearest. Used in '01 Matrix' (nearest 0), 'Rotting Oranges' (spread from all rotten oranges simultaneously), and similar propagation problems.

sections.title: Complexity
sections.time: O(V + E) for BFS, O(n) for monotonic deque sliding window
sections.space: O(V) for BFS queue and visited set, O(k) for monotonic deque
sections.explanation: BFS visits each vertex once and traverses each edge once - O(V + E). The visited set ensures no vertex is enqueued more than once. For the monotonic deque, each element is added to the deque exactly once and removed at most once (from either end), giving O(n) total work across the entire sliding window traversal. The deque holds at most k indices at any time.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Using `arr.shift()` for dequeue in performance-critical BFS: `shift` is O(n) in JavaScript because it shifts all remaining elements. For n=10⁵ nodes, this turns O(n) BFS into O(n²). Use a `head` pointer and increment it instead of shifting.

Marking nodes visited after dequeue instead of before enqueue: if you mark `visited[node] = true` when popping from the queue, a node can be enqueued multiple times (once for each neighbor that discovers it before it's processed). Mark immediately when pushing to prevent duplicate enqueues.

Confusing BFS queue order with DFS stack order: BFS with a queue processes nodes in order of increasing distance. Accidentally using a stack (LIFO) instead of a queue (FIFO) produces DFS traversal - correct paths but wrong distances, causing 'shortest path' problems to return wrong answers.

Forgetting to reset the visited set between multiple independent BFS calls: if your solution runs BFS from multiple source nodes in sequence (not multi-source BFS), each new BFS must start with a fresh visited set, or nodes from previous runs appear already-visited and are incorrectly skipped.

Off-by-one in level size for level-order: computing `levelSize = queue.length` dynamically inside the level loop (instead of computing it once at the start of each level as `const levelSize = queue.length - head`) picks up nodes enqueued in the current level, inflating the level size.

sections.title: What to Learn Next
sections.why: Linked lists are the foundational pointer-based data structure - the pointer manipulation you'll practice there (rewiring nodes, detecting cycles) is the exact skill that carries over to trees and graphs, where every edge is a pointer.
